steps.title: Primary and secondary
steps.body:
**Primary databases** hold submitted experimental data: **GenBank (NCBI), EMBL-ENA and DDBJ** (the INSDC trio exchange nucleotide sequences daily), **PDB** (3D structures from X-ray, NMR, cryo-EM), **GEO/SRA** (expression and raw reads).

**Secondary (curated/derived)**: **RefSeq** (non-redundant reference), **UniProt** (Swiss-Prot = manually reviewed; TrEMBL = automatically annotated), **Pfam/InterPro** (domains), **KEGG/Reactome** (pathways), **GO** (ontology), **PubMed** (literature).

steps.title: Two solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1 (Entrez query).** To find human BRCA1 mRNA records: `BRCA1[Gene] AND Homo sapiens[Organism] AND mRNA[Filter]`.

**Ex 2 (accessions).** RefSeq prefixes: **NM_** curated mRNA, **NP_** curated protein, **NC_** chromosome, **XM_/XP_** computational predictions. So NM_000059 is a curated mRNA record.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating TrEMBL annotation as reviewed.
- Quoting a GI number (retired) instead of an accession.version.
- Forgetting that a database release changes; always record the date and version.

steps.title: FASTA format
steps.body: A FASTA record starts with **>** then an identifier and optional description; subsequent lines are the sequence (often wrapped at 60 or 80 characters). Multi-FASTA holds many records. FASTQ adds quality scores. GenBank flat files carry annotation (features, CDS, references).

steps.title: Two solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Record `>seq1 demo` + `ATGGCC` + `AAATAG`: ID = seq1; sequence = ATGGCCAAATAG; length **12**.

**Ex 2.** `header.split()[0]` returns only the first word of the header; `"".join(lines[1:])` merges wrapped lines.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to strip trailing newlines or Windows carriage returns.
- Counting the header characters as part of the sequence.
- Assuming one record per file.

lessons.title: Lab: GC content, melting temperature and reverse complement

scenes.text: A PCR primer must have balanced GC content and a known Tm.
The reverse primer needs the reverse complement of the target.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: **GC% = (G + C)/length × 100.** **Wallace rule** (short oligos up to about 14 nt): **Tm = 2(A+T) + 4(G+C) °C.** **Reverse complement**: reverse the string and replace A↔T, G↔C (the opposite strand read 5′→3′). Typical primers: 18–25 nt, GC 40–60%, Tm 55–65 °C by nearest-neighbour methods.

steps.title: Two solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** ATGCGCTAAT: G=2, C=2 → 4/10 = **40.0%** GC.

**Ex 2.** A 12-mer with 4 A/T and 8 G/C: Tm = 2×4 + 4×8 = **40 °C**. Reverse complement of ATGCGCTAAT = **ATTAGCGCAT**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reversing without complementing (or the reverse).
- Using the Wallace rule for 25-mers (error is large).
- Forgetting that RNA has U instead of T.

print("".join(comp[b] for b in reversed(seq)))

steps.title: Reading frames
steps.body: A DNA strand has **3 forward** and **3 reverse** reading frames (6 total for double-stranded DNA). Stop codons: **TAA, TAG, TGA**. A real ORF has a long stretch without in-frame stops: random sequence has a stop about once every 64/3 ≈ 21 codons.

**Ex 2.** Frame 1 (start index 1): TGG CCT AAG GAT → 0 stops; frame 2: GGC CTA AGG ATG → 0 stops.

- Counting partial codons at the end.
- Assuming ATG is the only start (GTG, TTG are used by prokaryotes).

lessons.title: Monod kinetics: how substrate limits growth

scenes.text: In a Pune brewery lab, an E. coli-like culture grows fast on 10 g/L glucose but crawls as glucose runs low.
The process engineer needs one equation that predicts specific growth rate from substrate concentration.

steps.title: The Monod equation
steps.body:
Specific growth rate **μ = (1/X)(dX/dt)** has units h⁻¹. Monod (1942) proposed **μ = μmax·S / (Ks + S)**.

- **μmax**: maximum specific growth rate (h⁻¹), reached when S >> Ks.
- **Ks**: saturation constant = the S at which μ = μmax/2 (g/L).
- At low S, μ ≈ (μmax/Ks)·S (first order); at high S, μ ≈ μmax (zero order).

It is empirical, like Michaelis–Menten, and assumes one limiting substrate and no inhibition.

steps.title: Two solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** μmax = 0.5 h⁻¹, Ks = 0.2 g/L, S = 1.8 g/L.
Step 1: Ks + S = 2.0. Step 2: μ = 0.5 × 1.8 / 2.0 = **0.45 h⁻¹**.

**Ex 2.** What is μ when S = Ks? μ = μmax·Ks/(2Ks) = **μmax/2 = 0.25 h⁻¹** for the same organism.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating Ks as the concentration giving μmax. It gives half of μmax.
- Mixing units: S in mg/L but Ks in g/L.
- Using Monod when a product or substrate inhibits growth (Haldane/Andrews form is needed).

lessons.title: Batch growth curve, doubling time and biomass at time t

scenes.text: A student inoculates 0.05 g/L biomass and wants to know when the culture will be dense enough to transfer.
She plots ln X against time and finds a straight line.

steps.title: Phases of batch growth
steps.body:
1. **Lag**: cells adapt, no net growth.
2. **Exponential (log)**: μ = μmax, dX/dt = μX, so **X = X0·e^(μt)** and ln X is linear in t with slope μ.
3. **Deceleration**: substrate falling, μ drops.
4. **Stationary**: growth balances death or a nutrient is exhausted.
5. **Death**: net loss of viable cells.

**Doubling time td = ln2 / μ = 0.693/μ.**

steps.title: Two solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** X0 = 0.05 g/L, μ = 0.4 h⁻¹, t = 6 h in exponential phase. X = 0.05·e^(2.4) = 0.05 × 11.023 = **0.551 g/L**.

**Ex 2.** μ = 0.693 h⁻¹ gives td = 0.693/0.693 = **1.0 h**. A 30 min doubling time corresponds to μ = 0.693/0.5 = 1.386 h⁻¹.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using log10 values with an e-based equation without converting (ln = 2.303 log10).
- Applying X = X0e^(μt) through the lag phase; measure t from the end of lag.
- Confusing td (time) with μ (rate).

lessons.title: Yield coefficients and material balances

scenes.text: A fermentation uses 12 g/L glucose, yet biomass rises only 5 g/L.
The rest went to CO2, heat and products. A yield coefficient quantifies that split.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
**Y(X/S) = ΔX / ΔS** (g biomass formed per g substrate consumed). Similarly **Y(P/S) = ΔP/ΔS** and **Y(X/O2) = ΔX/ΔO2**.

Typical aerobic yields on glucose are about 0.4–0.5 g/g; anaerobic yields are lower (about 0.1) because less ATP is made per glucose.

Final biomass in batch when S is fully used: **X = X0 + Y(X/S)(S0 − S)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using S0 instead of ΔS when substrate is not exhausted.
- Mixing dry-weight and wet-weight biomass.
- Assuming the yield is constant: it falls with maintenance at low μ.

lessons.title: Maintenance energy and Pirt's equation; product formation

scenes.text: A slow chemostat culture shows an observed yield well below the true growth yield.
Part of the substrate pays for maintenance, not new cells.

steps.title: Pirt model
steps.body:
Substrate uptake: **qS = μ/Yg + m**, where Yg = true growth yield (g/g) and m = maintenance coefficient (g substrate per g biomass per h).

Dividing by μ: **1/Yobs = 1/Yg + m/μ**. A plot of 1/Yobs vs 1/μ is a straight line with intercept 1/Yg and slope m.

**Luedeking–Piret** for products: dP/dt = α(dX/dt) + βX. β = 0: growth-associated (e.g. ethanol, primary metabolites); α = 0: non-growth-associated (e.g. many antibiotics).

steps.title: Two solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Yg = 0.5, m = 0.04, μ = 0.2: 1/Y = 2 + 0.04/0.2 = 2.2, so Y = **0.4545 g/g**.

**Ex 2.** Same organism at μ = 0.4: 1/Y = 2 + 0.1 = 2.1, so Y = **0.476 g/g**. Faster growth means maintenance is a smaller share, so yield rises.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking Yobs is constant.
- Forgetting that m has units of h⁻¹ (g/g/h).
- Calling a secondary metabolite growth-associated: antibiotics usually form in stationary phase.

lessons.title: The downstream train: yield and purification fold

scenes.text: A biopharma plant in Hyderabad makes 10 kg of antibody per batch in the bioreactor.

steps.title: Stages
steps.body:
Downstream processing (DSP) turns broth into a pure, stable product. Classic four stages: **(1) removal of insolubles** (centrifugation, filtration), **(2) isolation** (extraction, adsorption, precipitation, UF), **(3) purification** (chromatography, crystallisation), **(4) polishing** (final chromatography, sterile filtration, drying, formulation).

DSP is commonly quoted as a large share (often well over half) of manufacturing cost for biologics, and purity needs rise with the end use: industrial enzyme < food < injectable.

**Step yield = product out / product in.** **Overall yield = product of step yields.** **Purification fold = final specific activity / initial specific activity** (specific activity = units per mg protein).

steps.title: Two solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Six steps each 85% yield: 0.85⁶ = **0.377**, only 37.7% survives. Cutting one step lifts yield to 0.85⁵ = 44.4%.

**Ex 2.** Specific activity rises from 2 U/mg to 80 U/mg: fold = 80/2 = **40**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Averaging step yields instead of multiplying.
- Reporting purification fold from total activity rather than specific activity.
- Adding steps for 'safety' without counting their yield loss.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
**Mechanical**: high-pressure homogeniser, bead mill (for yeast, fungi), sonication (lab scale; heat), French press. **Non-mechanical**: enzymatic (lysozyme for bacteria, lyticase for yeast), osmotic shock, detergents, freeze–thaw, alkali.

Gram-positive walls (thick peptidoglycan) and yeast walls resist more than Gram-negative cells. For homogenisers the fraction released per pass is first order: **R = Rm(1 − e^(−k·N))**, so the number of passes for a target R is N = −ln(1 − R/Rm)/k. Release depends strongly on pressure (k ∝ P^a) and cell type.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Over-disrupting, which makes fine debris that blocks separation and releases proteases and nucleic acids.
- Ignoring heat: cool the feed or use cooled valves.
- Using sonication at plant scale.

steps.title: Settling
steps.body:
Stokes' law (creeping flow): **vg = d²(ρp − ρl)g / (18μ)**. In a centrifuge replace g by ω²r. The **Σ factor** is the equivalent area of a gravity settling tank with the same performance, so **Q = 2·vg·Σ** (m³/s, vg in m/s, Σ in m²).

Scale-up: equal Q/Σ gives equal clarification. Disc-stack machines suit cells; decanters suit coarse solids; tubular bowls suit fine particles at small scale.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using d in µm without converting to metres.
- Using Stokes' law at high Reynolds number or with hindered settling.
- Forgetting the factor 2 in Q = 2vgΣ.

steps.title: Nucleotide chemistry
steps.body: A nucleotide = nitrogenous base + pentose sugar + 1–3 phosphates. In DNA the sugar is 2'-deoxyribose, in RNA ribose. Purines (A, G) have two fused rings; pyrimidines (C, T, U) have one. The base joins C1' of the sugar through an N-glycosidic bond; phosphates join C5'. Successive nucleotides are linked by 3'→5' phosphodiester bonds.

steps.title: Chargaff's rules
steps.body: For double-stranded DNA: **A = T**, **G = C**, so purines = pyrimidines (A+G = T+C = 50%). A–T pairs have 2 hydrogen bonds, G–C pairs have 3. The ratio (A+T)/(G+C) is species specific; the rules do not hold for single-stranded DNA or RNA.

steps.title: Solved example 2

1. A = T = 700 pairs of A–T → 700 × 2 = 1400 bonds.
2. G–C pairs = 2000 − 700 = 1300 → 1300 × 3 = 3900 bonds.
3. Total = 5300 hydrogen bonds.

- Counting bases instead of base pairs: 2000 bp has 4000 nucleotides.
- Forgetting that %GC, not %AT, controls stability.

lessons.title: The double helix: B, A and Z forms

scenes.text: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction photograph showed a helical pattern with a 3.4 Å repeat and a 34 Å pitch.
Watson and Crick built a model: two antiparallel strands, bases inside, sugar–phosphate backbone outside.

steps.title: B-DNA (Watson–Crick)
steps.body: Right-handed, 10.5 bp per turn (≈10 in the classic model), rise 3.4 Å per bp, pitch 34–35.7 Å, diameter 20 Å, with a wide major groove and a narrow minor groove. Strands are antiparallel (5'→3' opposite). Stabilised by hydrogen bonding **and** base stacking (hydrophobic and van der Waals), not by H-bonds alone.

steps.title: A-DNA and Z-DNA
steps.body: **A-form**: right-handed, 11 bp/turn, base pairs tilted, deep narrow major groove; seen in dehydrated DNA and in RNA–DNA hybrids and dsRNA. **Z-form**: left-handed zig-zag, 12 bp/turn, favoured by alternating purine–pyrimidine (e.g. CGCGCG) and high salt or negative supercoiling.

- Saying the minor groove is where most proteins read sequence; the major groove carries more chemical information.

steps.title: Linking number
steps.body: For a covalently closed circular DNA: **Lk = Tw + Wr** (linking number = twist + writhe). Lk is an integer and can change only by cutting a strand. Relaxed Lk₀ = N/h where h ≈ 10.5 bp/turn. **ΔLk = Lk − Lk₀**; **superhelical density σ = ΔLk/Lk₀** (natural plasmids ≈ −0.05 to −0.06, negative).

steps.title: Topoisomerases
steps.body: **Type I** cut one strand, change Lk by ±1 and need no ATP (E. coli topo I relaxes negative supercoils). **Type II** cut both strands and change Lk by ±2; they use ATP. **DNA gyrase** (bacterial type II) introduces negative supercoils and is the target of quinolones and novobiocin; topo IV decatenates daughter chromosomes. Eukaryotic topo II is a target of etoposide, topo I of camptothecin.

Each cycle changes Lk by −2, so Lk = 396. Since Tw stays 400, Wr = 396 − 400 = −4.

steps.title: Classes

- **rRNA** (~80% of cellular RNA): prokaryotic ribosome 70S = 30S (16S) + 50S (23S, 5S); eukaryotic 80S = 40S (18S) + 60S (28S, 5.8S, 5S).

- **mRNA** (~3–5%): coding template; eukaryotic mRNA has 5' cap and poly(A) tail.

lessons.title: Lab: Meselson–Stahl and the mode of replication

scenes.text: In 1958 Meselson and Stahl grew E. coli in ¹⁵N medium, shifted it to ¹⁴N and separated DNA by CsCl density-gradient centrifugation.
After one generation all DNA formed a single band of intermediate density; this ruled out conservative replication.

steps.title: Three models
steps.body: **Conservative**: parental duplex stays intact and a wholly new duplex forms. **Dispersive**: daughter strands are patchworks. **Semi-conservative**: each daughter duplex has one parental and one new strand. Results: gen 0 heavy band; gen 1 one hybrid band (kills conservative); gen 2 half hybrid, half light bands (kills dispersive); later generations: hybrid fraction falls, light fraction grows.

steps.title: Quantitative rule
steps.body: Starting from one ¹⁵N/¹⁵N duplex and growing in ¹⁴N, after n generations there are 2ⁿ duplexes; always exactly **2** contain a parental ¹⁵N strand (hybrids). Hybrid fraction = 2/2ⁿ = 2¹⁻ⁿ; light fraction = 1 − 2¹⁻ⁿ.

steps.title: Solved example 1

2³ = 8 duplexes; hybrids = 2 → 25%; light = 6 → 75%; no heavy.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
After how many generations is 3.125% of DNA hybrid?

2/2ⁿ = 0.03125 → 2ⁿ = 64 → n = 6.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying generation 1 kills the dispersive model: dispersive also gives one intermediate band; generation 2 distinguishes it.
- Forgetting that ¹⁵N strands are never destroyed, only diluted.
- Using 1/2ⁿ instead of 2/2ⁿ.

steps.body:
- **DnaA** binds oriC and melts AT-rich 13-mers.
- **DnaB** helicase (loaded by DnaC) unwinds ahead of the fork.
- **SSB** protects single strands; **gyrase** removes positive supercoils ahead.
- **Primase (DnaG)** makes ~10 nt RNA primers.
- **DNA Pol III** holoenzyme: core (α polymerase, ε 3'→5' exonuclease, θ), β sliding clamp (loaded by the clamp loader γ-complex) for processivity.
- **DNA Pol I** removes primers by 5'→3' exonuclease and fills gaps (nick translation); **DNA ligase** (NAD⁺-dependent in bacteria) seals nicks.

steps.title: Leading and lagging strand
steps.body: DNA polymerases synthesise only 5'→3' and need a 3'-OH. The leading strand is continuous; the lagging strand is made as **Okazaki fragments** (1000–2000 nt in bacteria, 100–200 nt in eukaryotes) which are primed, extended, then joined. Replication is semi-discontinuous, bidirectional and semi-conservative.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Time to copy the E. coli genome with two forks at 1000 nt/s.

Each fork copies 4.6×10⁶/2 = 2.3×10⁶ bp, t = 2.3×10⁶/1000 = 2300 s ≈ 38 min.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Okazaki fragments on one fork's lagging strand if 2.3×10⁶ nt are copied in 1000-nt pieces: 2300 fragments, needing 2300 RNA primers on that strand.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling DNA Pol I the main replicative enzyme (it is Pol III).
- Saying the lagging strand is made 3'→5'; it is 5'→3' in backstitched pieces.
- Forgetting that two forks halve the time.

lessons.title: Lab: Eukaryotic replication and origins

scenes.text: A human cell copies its genome in S phase (~8 h) using tens of thousands of origins.
Origins are licensed in G1 and fired in S so that no region replicates twice per cycle.

steps.title: Licensing and firing
steps.body: ORC binds origins; Cdc6 and Cdt1 load the MCM2–7 helicase to form the pre-replicative complex (G1, low CDK). In S phase CDK and DDK activate MCM with Cdc45 and GINS (the CMG helicase). Rising CDK blocks re-licensing, ensuring once-per-cycle replication.

steps.title: Polymerases
steps.body: Pol α/primase makes RNA–DNA primer; **Pol δ** (lagging) and **Pol ε** (leading) are the main replicative enzymes; PCNA is the clamp, RFC the clamp loader; FEN1 and RNase H remove primers; DNA ligase I seals. Eukaryotic forks move ~50 nt/s, so many origins are needed. Pol γ replicates mitochondrial DNA. Histones are recycled and new ones deposited by CAF-1.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
A human genome of 3.2×10⁹ bp copied from a single origin with two forks at 50 nt/s.

Each fork: 1.6×10⁹/50 = 3.2×10⁷ s ≈ 370 days. Hence thousands of origins.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Origins spaced evenly 100 kb apart in 3.2×10⁹ bp: number = 32,000. Each fork covers 50 kb: 50,000/50 = 1000 s ≈ 17 min if all fired together (in reality firing is staggered over ~8 h).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating Pol α with the main replicative polymerase.
- Saying MCM is loaded in S phase (it is loaded in G1).
- Confusing PCNA (eukaryote clamp) with β clamp (bacterial).

lessons.title: Lab: Telomeres, the end-replication problem and telomerase

scenes.text: Linear chromosomes end in tandem repeats, TTAGGG in humans, up to 5–15 kb long.
Normal somatic cells lose 50–100 bp per division and stop dividing at the Hayflick limit.

steps.title: End-replication problem
steps.body: After the last RNA primer on the lagging strand is removed, the 5' end of the new strand cannot be filled in because no 3'-OH is available, so each round leaves a shortened 3' overhang and a shorter chromosome. Shelterin proteins (TRF1, TRF2, POT1) and the T-loop protect ends from being seen as double-strand breaks.

steps.title: Telomerase
steps.body: A ribonucleoprotein: **TERT** (reverse transcriptase) plus **TERC** (RNA template, contains 3'-CAAUCCCAAUC-5'). It extends the 3' overhang using its own RNA template, then Pol α/primase fills in the complementary strand. Telomerase is active in germ cells, stem cells and ~85–90% of cancers; ALT is the alternative pathway.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A cell has 10,000 bp telomeres, loses 100 bp per division and senesces at 4,000 bp. Divisions left: (10,000 − 4,000)/100 = 60.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: If telomerase adds 150 bp per cycle and 100 bp is lost, net change = +50 bp per division; telomeres lengthen.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying telomerase is a DNA-dependent polymerase; it is an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase.
- Placing the gap at the leading strand end; the problem is on the lagging strand.
- Assuming telomerase carries out all lengthening in all cancers.

lessons.title: Lab: Fidelity, DNA repair pathways and recombination

scenes.text: UV light fuses adjacent thymines into cyclobutane dimers; xeroderma pigmentosum patients lack nucleotide excision repair.
A cell has several repair kits and must choose the right one for each lesion.

steps.title: Fidelity layers
steps.body: Base selection error ≈ 10⁻⁵, 3'→5' proofreading improves by ~10², mismatch repair (MMR) by another ~10²: overall ≈ 10⁻⁹ per bp per replication. E. coli MMR: MutS recognises mismatch, MutL recruits MutH, which nicks the unmethylated (new) strand at GATC (Dam methylation distinguishes strands). Human homologues MSH2/MLH1 – defects cause Lynch syndrome.

steps.title: Repair pathways
steps.body:
- **Direct reversal**: photolyase (cyclobutane dimers), O⁶-methylguanine methyltransferase.
- **BER**: DNA glycosylase removes damaged base (uracil, 8-oxoG) → AP endonuclease → Pol β/I + ligase.
- **NER**: bulky lesions/UV; UvrA/B/C in bacteria cut ~12–13 nt, XP proteins in humans.
- **MMR**: replication errors.
- **DSB repair**: non-homologous end joining (Ku70/80, DNA-PK, ligase IV, error-prone, G1) vs homologous recombination (BRCA1/2, Rad51/RecA, accurate, S/G2).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Genome 4.6×10⁶ bp, overall fidelity 10⁻⁹: expected errors per replication = 4.6×10⁶ × 10⁻⁹ = 0.0046, roughly one error per 217 divisions.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Without MMR the error rate is 10⁻⁷: 4.6×10⁶ × 10⁻⁷ = 0.46 errors per replication, 100 times more mutations.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using NER for single deaminated bases (BER does that).
- Saying NHEJ needs a template; HR does.
- Forgetting that mismatch repair must know which strand is new.

lessons.title: Lab: Bacterial RNA polymerase and promoter recognition

scenes.text: A bioinformatics student scans an E. coli upstream region for the signals RNA polymerase recognises.
She looks for the −35 and −10 boxes separated by a spacer of about 17 bp.

steps.title: RNA polymerase holoenzyme
steps.body: E. coli core enzyme = α₂ββ'ω (α: assembly and UP-element binding; β: catalysis, target of rifampicin; β': binds template DNA). The **σ factor** (σ⁷⁰ for housekeeping genes) binds core to give the holoenzyme, recognises the promoter and is released after ~10 nt are made. No primer is needed and there is no proofreading exonuclease.

steps.title: Promoter and initiation
steps.body: Consensus: **−35 TTGACA**, spacer 16–18 bp, **−10 TATAAT (Pribnow box)**, transcription start +1 (usually a purine). Closed complex → open complex (≈12–14 bp melted) → abortive initiation (short transcripts) → promoter clearance. Strong promoters resemble consensus; an AT-rich UP element upstream boosts α binding. Alternative σ factors (σ³², σ⁵⁴, σ^S) switch gene sets for heat shock, nitrogen limitation or stationary phase.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Sequence GGTTGACAGCTAGCTCAGTCCTAGGTATAATGCTAGC. −35 box TTGACA starts at index 2 (ends at index 7). −10 box TATAAT starts at index 25. Spacer = 25 − 8 = 17 bp, within the normal 16–18 bp.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Rifampicin binds the β subunit and blocks the exit channel after ~2–3 nt, so it inhibits initiation/early elongation; mutations in rpoB give resistance (used for M. tuberculosis therapy).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying σ remains bound during elongation.
- Counting the box start rather than the gap when measuring spacers.
- Believing RNA polymerase needs helicase to open the promoter; it melts DNA itself.

scenes.text: Death-cap mushroom toxin α-amanitin kills by blocking one eukaryotic RNA polymerase.
Different polymerases transcribe different gene classes in the nucleus and nucleolus.

steps.title: Polymerases
steps.body:
- **Pol I** (nucleolus): 45S pre-rRNA → 18S, 5.8S, 28S; insensitive to α-amanitin.
- **Pol II** (nucleoplasm): pre-mRNA, most snRNA, miRNA, lncRNA; very sensitive to α-amanitin (low µg/mL); has CTD of repeats YSPTSPS whose phosphorylation (Ser5 → Ser2) coordinates capping, splicing, 3' processing.
- **Pol III**: tRNA, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA; moderately sensitive.
Mitochondria use a single-subunit phage-like polymerase. Pol IV/V in plants make siRNA.

steps.title: Core promoter and GTFs
steps.body: Pol II core promoter: TATA box (~−25), Inr at +1, BRE, DPE. Assembly: **TFIID** (TBP binds TATA minor groove, bending DNA) → TFIIA, TFIIB → Pol II·TFIIF → TFIIE → TFIIH (helicase XPB opens DNA using ATP; kinase phosphorylates the CTD). Enhancers, activators, Mediator and chromatin remodellers regulate rate. CpG islands mark many promoters of housekeeping genes lacking TATA.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Which polymerase is affected if a cell treated with low-dose α-amanitin still makes 28S rRNA but not mRNA? Pol I is insensitive and makes rRNA; Pol II is blocked; therefore mRNA synthesis stops.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Cell lacks TFIIH kinase activity: initiation can occur but the CTD is not phosphorylated, impairing promoter escape and processing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing TATA box at −10 (that is the bacterial box).
- Saying Pol III makes mRNA.
- Confusing TBP (a subunit of TFIID) with TFIIB.

lessons.title: Lab: Capping, polyadenylation and splicing

scenes.text: A human gene may be 30,000 nt long, but its mature mRNA only 2,000 nt, the rest being introns.
Splicing releases introns as lariats.

steps.title: Cap and tail
steps.body: The **5' cap** (7-methylguanosine joined by a 5'–5' triphosphate; added co-transcriptionally by capping enzyme and methyltransferase) protects against exonucleases and aids ribosome binding. The **poly(A) tail** (~200 A in mammals) is added after cleavage ~10–30 nt downstream of **AAUAAA** (CPSF, CstF, CF I/II; poly(A) polymerase); it stabilises mRNA and aids translation. Histone mRNAs lack tails.

steps.title: Splicing
steps.body: Introns begin with **GU** at the 5' splice site and end with **AG** at the 3' end, with a branch-point adenosine and polypyrimidine tract upstream. Two transesterifications: (1) branch A 2'-OH attacks the 5' splice site → lariat intermediate; (2) free exon 3'-OH attacks the 3' splice site → exons joined, lariat released. The spliceosome (U1, U2, U4/U6, U5 snRNPs + proteins; ATP-dependent) catalyses it. Group I/II introns self-splice. Alternative splicing (exon skipping, alternative 5'/3' sites, intron retention, mutually exclusive exons) lets one gene give many proteins.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Pre-mRNA 5,400 nt with introns of 1,200, 900 and 1,500 nt. Exons = 5,400 − 3,600 = 1,800 nt. Add a 200 nt poly(A) tail: mature transcript ≈ 2,000 nt. Number of exons = 4.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A gene has 3 independent cassette exons that can be included or skipped: 2³ = 8 possible isoforms.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the cap is added at the 3' end.
- Forgetting that splicing is not a hydrolysis: it is two transesterifications.
- Mixing up GU (5' splice site) and AG (3' splice site).

scenes.text: Rifampicin treats tuberculosis; actinomycin D is used in some chemotherapy and in the lab to shut down transcription.

steps.title: Maturation of stable RNAs
steps.body: Bacterial 30S precursor is cut by RNases III, E, P and others into 16S, 23S, 5S and tRNAs. RNase P (a ribozyme) trims 5' ends of tRNA; CCA is added by tRNA nucleotidyltransferase if absent; many bases are modified (pseudouridine, inosine, ribothymidine). Eukaryotic 45S pre-rRNA is processed in the nucleolus with snoRNAs guiding 2'-O-methylation and pseudouridylation. tRNAs may have introns.

steps.title: RNA editing and inhibitors
steps.body: Editing examples: apoB mRNA C→U by APOBEC1 gives a truncated apoB-48 in intestine (apoB-100 in liver); ADAR A→I editing. Inhibitors: **rifampicin** (β subunit, bacterial initiation); **actinomycin D** intercalates into dsDNA, blocking elongation in all cells; **α-amanitin** (Pol II); **cordycepin** (3'-deoxyadenosine, chain terminator).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A liver apoB-100 mRNA has CAA at codon 2153. Editing C→U gives UAA, a stop codon, so the intestine makes the shorter apoB-48 (about 48% of the length).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Why does actinomycin D stop both bacterial and eukaryotic transcription while rifampicin stops only bacterial? Actinomycin binds DNA (universal); rifampicin binds the bacterial β subunit, structurally different from eukaryotic enzymes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying rifampicin is a DNA intercalator.
- Treating editing as a DNA mutation; it changes RNA only.
- Thinking all tRNAs contain CCA genetically encoded in eukaryotes.

lessons.title: Lab: Reading the genetic code

scenes.text: In 1961 Nirenberg and Matthaei showed that poly-U RNA made a poly-phenylalanine peptide in a cell-free system.
Today you translate an mRNA with a few lines of code.

steps.title: Properties of the code
steps.body: Triplet (4³ = 64 codons), **non-overlapping**, **commaless**, **degenerate** (61 sense codons for 20 amino acids), **unambiguous** (one codon, one amino acid), **nearly universal**. Start: AUG (Met; fMet in bacteria). Stop: UAA (ochre), UAG (amber), UGA (opal). Degeneracy is mostly in the third base. Exceptions: human mitochondria read UGA as Trp and AUA as Met; selenocysteine uses UGA with a SECIS element.

steps.title: Frameshifts and point mutations
steps.body: Silent (same amino acid), missense (different amino acid), nonsense (stop) mutations. Insertion/deletion not a multiple of 3 shifts the reading frame (frameshift); multiples of 3 add/remove whole amino acids. Crick's experiments with T4 rII: +1 and −1 cancel; three +1 insertions restore the frame.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Translate 5'-AUG UUU GGC UAA-3' using AUG=Met(M), UUU=Phe(F), GGC=Gly(G), UAA=stop. Protein: M–F–G (3 aa).

steps.title: Solved example 2

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting the stop codon as an amino acid.
- Saying the code is ambiguous because it is degenerate. Degenerate = many codons per amino acid; ambiguous would be one codon, many amino acids.
- Forgetting to find AUG first and reading in the right frame.

lessons.title: Lab: Initiation, elongation and termination on the ribosome

scenes.text: A bacterial ribosome can add about 15–20 amino acids per second.
Each cycle uses the A, P and E sites.

steps.title: Bacterial initiation
steps.body: 30S binds mRNA through the **Shine–Dalgarno** sequence (5'-AGGAGG-3', ~7 nt upstream of AUG) pairing with 16S rRNA; IF3 prevents early subunit joining, IF1 blocks A site, IF2·GTP delivers **fMet-tRNA^fMet** to the P site. 50S joins, GTP hydrolysis releases the factors → 70S initiation complex.

steps.title: Elongation and termination
steps.body: **Elongation**: EF-Tu·GTP delivers aminoacyl-tRNA to the A site; correct codon triggers GTP hydrolysis; peptidyl transferase (23S rRNA) forms the peptide bond (chain moves to A-site tRNA); **EF-G·GTP** translocates the ribosome one codon, moving tRNAs to P and E. **Termination**: stop codon in A site is recognised by RF1 (UAA, UAG) or RF2 (UAA, UGA); the peptide is hydrolysed; RF3·GTP and RRF with EF-G recycle ribosomes. Eukaryotes: Met-tRNAi, eIF4E binds cap, eIF4G–PABP circularise mRNA, 43S scans for the first AUG in Kozak context (GCCRCCAUGG), one eRF1 recognises all stops.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Time to translate a 450-aa protein at 15 aa/s: 450/15 = 30 s.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: mRNA 5'-...AGGAGGUUACAUAUGAAA...: AUG is the first start; Shine–Dalgarno ends 7 nt upstream; spacing is typical (5–9 nt). Using the wrong frame would lose the protein, so spacing and start codon choice matter.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using EF-Tu for translocation (that is EF-G).
- Placing the first tRNA in the A site; initiator goes into the P site.
- Saying peptide bond formation requires GTP; it is catalysed by rRNA and needs none.

lessons.title: Lab: Energetics and numericals of translation

scenes.text: Protein synthesis is the most energy-consuming process in a growing cell.
We count high-energy phosphate bonds and nucleotides.

steps.title: Accounting
steps.body: Per residue: 2 high-energy bonds for aminoacylation (ATP → AMP + PPi), 1 GTP for EF-Tu delivery, 1 GTP for EF-G translocation = 4 per peptide bond. Overhead: 1 GTP for initiation (IF2) and 1 for termination (RF3) in the simple textbook model. Average amino acid mass ≈ 110 Da. A gene with n amino acids has coding length 3n + 3 nt (stop included).

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: For a protein of n amino acids: bonds = 2n (charging) + 2(n − 1) (elongation) + 2 (IF2, RF3) = **4n**. Check n = 100 → 400.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: 100-residue peptide: charging 200 + elongation 99 × 2 = 198 + 2 = 400 high-energy bonds.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Protein of 300 residues: coding sequence = 300×3 + 3 = 903 nt; mass ≈ 300 × 110 = 33,000 Da = 33 kDa; time at 15 aa/s = 20 s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting ATP→ADP (1 bond) for charging instead of ATP→AMP (2).
- Counting the stop codon as an extra residue.
- Forgetting that mRNA length includes UTRs, not only the coding sequence.

lessons.title: Lab: The lac operon – induction and catabolite repression

scenes.text: E. coli grown on glucose ignores lactose, but when glucose runs out and lactose is present it switches on lactose genes within minutes.
François Jacob and Jacques Monod explained this with the operon model (Nobel Prize 1965).

steps.title: Structure and negative control
steps.body: lacZYA is one polycistronic mRNA: **lacZ** β-galactosidase, **lacY** permease, **lacA** transacetylase. Upstream: promoter P, operator O, and the repressor gene **lacI** with its own promoter. Without lactose, LacI tetramer binds O and blocks RNA polymerase. Allolactose (an isomer of lactose made by β-gal) binds LacI and releases it → induction. The gratuitous inducer **IPTG** is non-metabolisable.

steps.title: Positive control
steps.body: The lac promoter is weak; it needs **CAP·cAMP** (catabolite activator protein) binding upstream. When glucose is high, adenylate cyclase is inhibited, cAMP is low and CAP cannot bind, so even with lactose expression stays low (**catabolite repression**; diauxic growth). Full expression needs lactose present **and** glucose absent.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
+lactose, −glucose: allolactose frees repressor, cAMP high, CAP active → **high** expression (~100×).

+lactose, +glucose: repressor off but no CAP → low.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: −lactose, −glucose: CAP bound but repressor blocks operator → basal level (~1–3 mRNA/cell). −lactose, +glucose: repressed and no CAP → essentially off.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying lactose itself binds the repressor (allolactose does).
- Forgetting that glucose lowers cAMP.
- Thinking the operon makes three separate mRNAs; it is one polycistronic message.

scenes.text: Jacob and Monod introduced extra copies of lac genes on an F' plasmid to make partial diploids.
Whether a mutation acts in cis or in trans reveals what kind of gene it affects.

steps.title: Key mutant types
steps.body:
- **lacI⁻**: no functional repressor → constitutive expression; recessive and **trans-acting** (a wild-type lacI⁺ copy complements).
- **lacOᶜ**: operator cannot bind repressor → constitutive, **cis-dominant** (affects only the genes on the same DNA).
- **lacIˢ** (super-repressor): cannot bind allolactose → never induced; dominant over lacI⁺ in trans.
- **lacZ⁻ / lacY⁻**: loss of enzyme or permease; recessive, complemented in trans.
- **lacP⁻**: no transcription, cis-acting.

steps.title: How to solve
steps.body:
1. Note which genes sit on each DNA molecule (cis arrangement).
2. A repressor (diffusible protein) acts on both operators; operator or promoter mutations act only on their own DNA.
3. Check enzyme activity separately for each structural gene and for both conditions (±inducer).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Genotype I⁻ P⁺ O⁺ Z⁺ / F' I⁺ P⁺ O⁺ Z⁻: I⁺ on F' makes repressor that binds both operators; without inducer no β-gal; with inducer the chromosomal Z⁺ is expressed → inducible β-gal.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: I⁺ P⁺ Oᶜ Z⁻ / F' I⁺ P⁺ O⁺ Z⁺: Oᶜ is on the chromosome with Z⁻ so its constitutive transcription yields a defective Z; F' Z⁺ is controlled by O⁺ and is repressed without inducer → no active β-gal without inducer, inducible with inducer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming operator mutations can be complemented in trans.
- Forgetting that lacIˢ is dominant.
- Ignoring which Z allele sits next to which operator.

lessons.title: Lab: trp operon, attenuation and phage lambda switch

story.title: Turning genes off when the product is plentiful

scenes.text: E. coli stops making tryptophan enzymes when tryptophan is abundant.
Phage λ decides between lysis and lysogeny by a bistable genetic switch.

steps.title: trp operon
steps.body: A repressible operon (trpEDCBA). Tryptophan is the **corepressor**: it binds the aporepressor TrpR, which then binds operator. Additionally, **attenuation**: the leader region has four segments (1–4) and a Trp-rich leader peptide with two Trp codons. With high Trp, the ribosome moves through region 1 and covers 2, so 3–4 forms the terminator hairpin → transcription stops. With low Trp the ribosome stalls at the Trp codons, 2–3 pairs (antiterminator) and transcription continues. Because transcription and translation are coupled, attenuation exists only in bacteria.

steps.title: Lambda switch
steps.body: **cI** (repressor) maintains lysogeny and represses lytic genes via OR1–OR3 and PRM autoregulation; **Cro** promotes the lytic cycle. DNA damage activates RecA → cI auto-cleavage → Cro expressed → prophage induction (SOS). Low infection multiplicity and high protease CII favour lysogeny; starvation of host favours lysogeny.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: High tryptophan: ribosome translates leader quickly, region 2 is blocked, 3:4 terminator forms, short 140-nt leader transcript only → enzymes not made.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Lysogen exposed to UV: RecA* cleaves cI, repressor level falls below threshold, Cro binds OR3 and PRM shuts down → lytic development, cell lysis and ~100 phages released.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the trp operon inducible (it is repressible).
- Believing attenuation operates in eukaryotes.
- Mixing up cI (lysogeny) and Cro (lysis).

lessons.title: Lab: Chromatin and eukaryotic transcriptional control

story.title: Two metres in a six-micron nucleus

scenes.text: Each human cell contains about 2 m of DNA packed into a nucleus ~6 µm across.
Packaging itself regulates which genes are available.

steps.title: Nucleosome
steps.body: Histone octamer (two each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4) with 147 bp of DNA wound 1.65 times; linker DNA and H1 give ~200 bp repeat. Beads-on-a-string (11 nm) → 30-nm fibre (solenoid) → loops → scaffold → chromosome. Euchromatin is open and active; heterochromatin is condensed (constitutive and facultative). Compaction of DNA ≈ 10,000-fold in metaphase chromosomes.

steps.title: Control elements
steps.body: **Promoter-proximal elements**, **enhancers** (orientation- and distance-independent, bind activators; looping via Mediator/cohesin), **silencers**, **insulators** (CTCF). Activators have DNA-binding domains (helix-turn-helix, zinc finger, leucine zipper, bHLH) and activation domains; coactivators (HATs, SWI/SNF remodellers) open chromatin. Combinatorial control by a few factors creates many patterns; steroid receptors are ligand-activated transcription factors.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Nucleosomes in a haploid human genome (3.2×10⁹ bp, 200 bp per nucleosome repeat): 3.2×10⁹/200 = 1.6×10⁷.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Packing ratio: 2 m of DNA into a 6 µm nucleus is a linear reduction of 2/(6×10⁻⁶) ≈ 3.3×10⁵ (the length compaction is far smaller for a single metaphase chromosome, ~10⁴).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying histones are acidic (they are rich in Lys and Arg, so basic).
- Counting H1 as part of the octamer.
- Treating enhancers as always upstream.

lessons.title: Lab: PCR – design and amplification arithmetic

story.title: Copying a gene a billion times

scenes.text: A diagnostic lab amplifies a 450 bp viral target from a patient swab.
Each cycle ideally doubles the number of target molecules.

steps.title: The reaction
steps.body: Mix: template DNA, two primers (18–25 nt, 40–60% GC, similar Tm, no 3' complementarity), dNTPs, Mg²⁺, buffer and a **thermostable polymerase (Taq, from Thermus aquaticus**; proofreading Pfu/Phusion for cloning). Cycle: denaturation 94–95 °C (30 s) → annealing ≈ Tm − 5 °C (30 s) → extension 72 °C (≈1 min per kb). Typical 25–35 cycles; final extension 5–10 min. Controls: no-template and positive.

steps.title: Arithmetic
steps.body: Copies after n ideal cycles = N₀ × 2ⁿ. With efficiency E (0–1): N = N₀(1+E)ⁿ. The first cycles produce long products; target-length amplicons (defined by the primers) appear exponentially from cycle 3. Variants: RT-PCR (cDNA from RNA), nested PCR, multiplex, inverse PCR, colony PCR, hot-start.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: 100 template molecules, 5 ideal cycles: 100 × 2⁵ = 3200 copies.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Primer 5'-ATGCGTACCTGAAGCTTCAA-3' (20 nt): count G/C = 9? Letters: A T G C G T A C C T G A A G C T T C A A → G,C,G,C,C,G,G,C,C = 9 G/C, 11 A/T. Wallace Tm = 2×11 + 4×9 = 22 + 36 = 58 °C → anneal at ≈ 53 °C.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Annealing above the primer Tm (no product) or far below (non-specific bands).
- Using Taq when proofreading is required.
- Believing 30 cycles give exactly 2³⁰ copies; reagents and efficiency limit the plateau.

lessons.title: Lab: Agarose gel electrophoresis and blotting

scenes.text: A technician loads a ladder and a PCR product on a 1% agarose gel stained with a safe DNA dye.
She must estimate the product size from migration distance.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body: DNA is negatively charged and migrates toward the anode (+). Smaller fragments migrate faster through the agarose mesh. Migration distance is inversely proportional to **log₁₀(fragment size)**. Higher agarose % resolves smaller fragments (0.7% for 5–10 kb; 2% for 100–500 bp). Pulsed-field gels resolve >50 kb. Stains: ethidium bromide (mutagen!) or SYBR Safe. Supercoiled plasmid migrates fastest, then linear, then nicked circle.

steps.title: Blotting
steps.body: **Southern** (DNA, with DNA probe), **Northern** (RNA), **Western** (protein, with antibody) — transfer to nitrocellulose/nylon/PVDF, hybridise to labelled probe, detect. SDS-PAGE separates proteins by size (SDS gives uniform charge/mass); native PAGE retains charge; isoelectric focusing separates by pI; 2D gels combine both.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Ladder: 1000 bp at 20 mm and 100 bp at 40 mm. Log-linear: log 1000 = 3 at 20 mm, log 100 = 2 at 40 mm → slope = −1/20 per mm. Band at 30 mm: log size = 2.5 → size = 10².⁵ ≈ 316 bp.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A band at 25 mm: log size = 3 − (5/20) = 2.75 → 10².⁷⁵ ≈ 562 bp.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Plotting distance against size on a linear axis.
- Running the gel with the wrong polarity (DNA runs toward +).
- Using agarose % unsuited to fragment size.

lessons.title: Lab: Sanger and next-generation sequencing

scenes.text: The Human Genome Project took 13 years; today a genome can be sequenced in a day.
Planning a run means calculating coverage.

steps.title: Sanger chain termination
steps.body: Template, primer, DNA polymerase, dNTPs and a small amount of fluorescent **ddNTPs** (lacking 3'-OH) that terminate chains. Capillary electrophoresis separates fragments differing by one nucleotide; the order of terminal dyes gives the sequence read 5'→3' of the new strand (complementary to the template). Read length ≈ 800–1000 nt; accuracy ~99.99%.

steps.title: NGS and coverage
steps.body: Illumina: fragment library, bridge amplification, sequencing by synthesis with reversible terminators (short reads, 50–300 nt, very high throughput). Nanopore/PacBio give long reads. **Coverage (depth) = N × L / G** where N = reads, L = read length, G = genome size. Human whole-genome resequencing is typically 30×. Assembly: de novo vs reference mapping; N50 measures contiguity.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Reads needed for 30× coverage of a 3.2×10⁹ bp genome with 150 nt reads: N = 30 × 3.2×10⁹ / 150 = 6.4×10⁸ reads.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Bacterial genome 4.6 Mb, 100× coverage, 250 nt reads: N = 100 × 4.6×10⁶ / 250 = 1.84×10⁶ reads.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing the read strand with the template strand when writing the sequence.
- Treating coverage as the percentage of the genome covered (it is mean depth).
- Using ddNTPs at the same concentration as dNTPs (chains would all be tiny).

lessons.title: Lab: Isolation of genomic DNA from bacteria or plant tissue

scenes.text: Students lyse cells, remove proteins and precipitate DNA with cold ethanol.
Each reagent has a reason, and the viva will ask for it.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body: Lysis (lysozyme/EDTA for bacteria; CTAB or SDS for plants) → protein removal (proteinase K, or phenol:chloroform:isoamyl alcohol 25:24:1) → RNA removal (RNase A) → precipitation (1/10 volume 3 M sodium acetate pH 5.2 + 2–2.5 volumes ice-cold ethanol; Na⁺ neutralises phosphates) → 70% ethanol wash → dissolve in TE. EDTA chelates Mg²⁺ and inhibits DNases.

steps.title: Safety and tips
steps.body: Phenol is corrosive; work in a fume hood with gloves. Avoid vortexing (shears DNA >20 kb). Spool high-molecular-weight DNA on a glass rod. Check yield and purity (A260/280) and integrity on 0.8% agarose.

steps.title: Observation example 1
steps.body: Spectrophotometer: A260 = 0.35, A280 = 0.19 (1:100 dilution). Ratio = 1.84 (pure). Concentration = 0.35 × 50 × 100 = 1,750 µg/mL.

steps.title: Observation example 2
steps.body: Total yield from 200 µL TE at 1,750 µg/mL = 0.2 mL × 1,750 µg/mL = 350 µg.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding ethanol before salt.
- Letting the pellet over-dry so that DNA will not redissolve.
- Forgetting RNase, leaving RNA contamination.

steps.title: Method

steps.title: Recipe per 25 µL reaction
steps.body: 10× buffer 2.5 µL; 10 mM dNTP mix 0.5 µL; forward primer (10 µM) 1.0 µL; reverse primer (10 µM) 1.0 µL; Taq (5 U/µL) 0.25 µL; template 1.0 µL; water 18.75 µL. - Omitting the no-template control.
- Pipetting too little for the last tube (no extra volume).

lessons.title: Lab: Totipotency and preparing MS medium

scenes.text: A tissue-culture student in Pune must prepare a litre of Murashige and Skoog (MS) medium for banana shoot tips.
She works out sugar, agar, pH and hormone volumes before sterilising.

steps.title: Principles
steps.body: **Totipotency** (Haberlandt, 1902): a living plant cell can regenerate a whole plant. An **explant** (shoot tip, leaf disc, node) is surface-sterilised (70% ethanol, then 0.1% HgCl₂ or 1–2% sodium hypochlorite) and placed on **MS medium** (Murashige and Skoog, 1962): macro and micro salts, vitamins (thiamine, myo-inositol), carbon source (**3% sucrose = 30 g/L**), gelling agent (**0.7–0.8% agar**), pH adjusted to **5.8** before autoclaving at **121 °C, 15 psi, 15–20 min**. Heat-labile additives (some hormones, antibiotics, vitamins) are filter-sterilised (0.22 µm) and added after cooling.

steps.title: Two solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** BAP stock 1 mg/mL; target 2 mg/L in 1 L: C1V1 = C2V2 → 1 mg/mL × V = 2 mg → **V = 2 mL**.

**Ex 2.** 0.8% agar for 500 mL: 0.8 g per 100 mL × 5 = **4 g**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adjusting pH after adding agar (it will not mix).
- Autoclaving heat-labile hormones such as GA₃ and zeatin.
- Overloading the autoclave so steam cannot penetrate.

lessons.title: Lab: Plant growth regulators and the Skoog–Miller ratio

scenes.text: Tobacco pith explants on identical media with different hormone ratios give roots, shoots or callus.
The ratio of auxin to cytokinin steers development.

steps.title: Hormones and ratios
steps.body:
**Auxins** (IAA, NAA, IBA, 2,4-D): cell elongation, callus induction, rooting. **Cytokinins** (BAP, kinetin, zeatin): cell division, shoot induction. **Gibberellins** (GA₃): elongation. **ABA**: dormancy, stress.

Skoog and Miller (1957): **high auxin : low cytokinin → roots; high cytokinin : low auxin → shoots; intermediate → undifferentiated callus.** 2,4-D is the usual callus inducer; it also drives somatic embryogenesis.

steps.title: Two solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** NAA 2 mg/L and BAP 0.5 mg/L: ratio 4:1, auxin-dominant, so expect **rooting** or callus.

**Ex 2.** BAP 3 mg/L, NAA 0.2 mg/L: ratio 1:15 → **shoot proliferation**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting one universal ratio: it depends on species and tissue.
- Using too much 2,4-D, which causes genetic abnormalities.
- Forgetting endogenous hormones in the explant.

lessons.title: Micropropagation: stages and multiplication arithmetic

story.title: A million bananas from one shoot tip

scenes.text: A nursery in Jalgaon multiplies disease-free banana plantlets in vitro.
The manager must forecast numbers per subculture cycle.

steps.title: Stages
steps.body:
**Stage 0** mother plant selection and preparation; **Stage I** establishment of aseptic culture; **Stage II** multiplication (axillary shoot proliferation, repeated subculture); **Stage III** rooting; **Stage IV** hardening/acclimatisation in greenhouse (high humidity, gradually reduced). Benefits: clonal, virus-free (meristem culture + thermotherapy), rapid, year-round, small space. Limits: cost, contamination, somaclonal variation, hyperhydricity (vitrification).

With multiplication rate m per cycle and n cycles: **N = m^n** (assuming no loss).

steps.title: Two solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** m = 4, n = 5: N = 4⁵ = **1024** shoots from one explant.

**Ex 2.** m = 3 per 4 weeks for 20 weeks (5 cycles): 3⁵ = **243**; with 15% loss in hardening, 243 × 0.85 ≈ **206** plants.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting contamination and hardening losses.
- Subculturing too many cycles, raising somaclonal variation.
- Using unsuitable explants (meristem is best for virus elimination).

lessons.title: Protoplasts, haploids, cryopreservation and synthetic seeds

scenes.text: A breeder wants a new hybrid between two sexually incompatible species.
Another team stores elite germplasm at −196 °C.

steps.title: Techniques
steps.body:
- **Protoplast culture and fusion**: remove cell wall with cellulase + pectinase in an osmoticum; fuse with PEG or electric pulse → **somatic hybrids** (e.g. pomato) and **cybrids**.
- **Haploid production**: **anther/microspore culture** → haploids (n); chromosome doubling with colchicine gives **doubled haploids**, fully homozygous in one generation.
- **Embryo rescue** saves hybrid embryos that abort.
- **Cryopreservation**: liquid nitrogen at **−196 °C** with cryoprotectants (DMSO, glycerol, sucrose), vitrification.
- **Synthetic (artificial) seeds**: somatic embryos encapsulated in **calcium alginate**.
- **Somaclonal variation**: heritable variation from culture; harmful for clonal propagation but a source of new traits (e.g. disease resistance).

steps.title: Two solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Rice has 2n = 24. Anther culture haploid: n = **12**; after colchicine doubling: **24**, homozygous.

**Ex 2.** Protoplast viability by FDA stain: 180 fluorescing in 200 = **90%**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using hypotonic solution for protoplasts (they burst).
- Treating doubled haploids as heterozygous.
- Forgetting cryoprotectants (ice crystals kill cells).
